chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Implied Volatility Actually Means

lessons.title: Historical Volatility vs Implied Volatility: Two Different Questions

children.text: Two Different Questions About the Same Word

Ask a trader what a stock's volatility is and you will get answers to two completely different questions, often without either side realizing it. One person means: how much has this stock actually moved over the last month, in hard historical fact. The other means: how much does the options market expect it to move over the weeks ahead, priced into every strike on the chain right now. Both get called volatility. They are rarely the same number, and confusing them is one of the fastest ways to misprice a trade.
Historical (Realized) Volatility: Measuring What Already Happened

Historical volatility, also called realized volatility, is a purely backward-looking statistic. You take a series of past daily returns for an underlying, say Nifty 50 closing prices over the last 30 trading days, compute the standard deviation of those daily log returns, then annualize it. There is no forecasting here and no option prices involved. It is arithmetic performed on data that has already happened.

body.caption: sigma-daily is the standard deviation of daily log returns over your lookback window. 252 is the standard annualization convention used across Indian and global derivatives desks (NSE's actual trading calendar runs closer to 245 to 250 sessions a year, but 252 is the convention almost everyone still uses).

children.text: Here is what that looks like with numbers. Say Nifty's daily log returns over the past 30 trading days had a standard deviation of 0.70%. Annualized realized volatility works out to 0.70% times the square root of 252, which is 0.70% times 15.87, or about 11.1%. That 11.1% is a fact about the past. It tells you nothing directly about what Nifty will do next week. It only tells you how choppy the last 30 sessions actually were.

children.text: Implied Volatility: Pricing What Has Not Happened Yet

Implied volatility runs in the opposite direction entirely. Instead of starting with past prices and computing a statistic, you start with today's live option premium on NSE, the one number everyone can see on the chain, and ask the pricing model: what volatility input would produce exactly this price? That single number, solved by working backward through the formula, is IV. It is forward-looking by construction. It exists only because a price already exists, and it changes the moment that price changes, even if the underlying itself has not moved an inch. The next lesson walks through the actual inversion mechanics; for now, hold onto this: IV is not measured from history, it is extracted from a price the market has already agreed on.

India VIX is the most visible implied volatility number in the Indian market, and it is worth being precise about what it actually is. NSE computes it from the live order book of near-month and next-month Nifty options, specifically their bid-ask quotes rather than last traded price, using a variance-based methodology licensed from the Chicago Board Options Exchange, the same family of maths behind the original US VIX. The output is a single annualized number representing the market's expectation of Nifty's volatility over the next 30 calendar days. It is not the implied volatility of one option. It is a weighted aggregate across a whole strip of out-of-the-money calls and puts.

body.text: India VIX does not measure how much Nifty has moved. It measures how much options traders are currently paying to be protected against how much Nifty might move next. A rising VIX with a flat Nifty is not a contradiction. It usually means the market has spotted a reason to worry that has not shown up in price yet.

children.text: Same Underlying, Two Different Numbers: The Volatility Risk Premium
Put realized volatility and implied volatility side by side on any given day and, more often than not, IV sits a little higher. This gap has a name: the
volatility risk premium

(VRP), and it is one of the best-documented patterns in options markets worldwide, India included. It exists because buying options is, in part, buying insurance, and insurance is priced to make money for the seller on average, not on every single policy.

markDefs.definition: The tendency for implied volatility to trade above the volatility that subsequently gets realized, on average and over time. It exists because option buyers are willing to pay extra for protection against large, painful moves, and option sellers demand compensation for underwriting that risk. It is a statistical tendency, not a guarantee on any single trade.

children.text: The VRP is a calm-market tendency, not a law. It compresses, disappears, or reverses entirely around known events, because IV does something realized volatility structurally cannot: it prices in a specific date on the calendar before that date arrives.
Where the Two Numbers Pull Apart: Event Risk

Take Union Budget day, the single most reliable volatility event on the Indian calendar. In the days before the Budget, Nifty might trade in its usual quiet 100 to 150-point daily range, which keeps realized volatility low and steady. But that week's option chain tells a completely different story. Traders know a big, binary, calendar-certain event is coming, and every strike gets bid up to reflect that. ATM IV for that week's expiry can jump 6 to 10 volatility points above its usual level, even though not a single extra Nifty point has actually moved yet. Realized volatility, being backward-looking, has no way to see this coming. Implied volatility, being forward-looking, is built to price almost nothing else.

body.caption: S is spot price, IV is the annualized implied volatility as a decimal, T is calendar days to expiry. This gives a rough one-standard-deviation move: roughly a 68% chance the underlying stays within this band by expiry, all figures here illustrative and approximate.

children.text: Apply this to Nifty at 24,800 with 7 calendar days to a normal weekly expiry and ATM IV of 14%. Expected move works out to 24,800 times 0.14 times the square root of (7 divided by 365), which is 24,800 times 0.14 times 0.1385, or roughly ₹481. Now redo the same calculation for a Budget-week expiry, same 7 days to go, but ATM IV has jumped to 22% on event pricing alone. Expected move becomes 24,800 times 0.22 times 0.1385, or roughly ₹756. Same index, same time to expiry, a ₹275 wider expected range, purely because IV moved and nothing else did.

body.title: Realized Volatility vs ATM Implied Volatility Across Market Regimes (Illustrative)

children.text: Notice the pattern. In a calm week, IV sits modestly above realized vol, the usual VRP. Heading into Budget week, IV jumps well ahead of realized vol because the market is pricing an event that has not happened yet. In the week right after the Budget, realized volatility can stay elevated since the actual move already happened, while IV collapses just as fast, because the uncertainty that was being priced is now resolved. An election result week can push IV even higher than Budget week, reflecting a genuinely more binary, harder-to-model outcome.
This is exactly what desks call
IV crush

: an option's implied volatility falling sharply right after the event it was pricing has passed, often even when the underlying moves a lot, because the uncertainty itself, not just the outcome, is what IV was charging for.

markDefs.definition: A sharp drop in an option's implied volatility right after a known, dated event resolves, since the uncertainty being priced is now gone. It can happen even when the underlying makes a large move, and it is a common reason a correct directional bet on an event still loses money.

body.text: Buying options purely to bet on a known event, expecting the move itself to make you money, ignores that you are paying an IV premium going in, and that premium can evaporate the moment the event is over, sometimes fast enough to erase gains from a correct directional call.

body.title: Reading the divergence
body.question: Nifty's 30-day realized volatility has been a steady 10% for three weeks. This week, ATM IV on the weekly Nifty options jumps to 24% while Nifty itself barely moves. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The realized volatility calculation is wrong and needs updating
The market is pricing in a specific upcoming event, such as a results announcement or policy decision, that has not happened yet
IV always equals double the realized volatility by convention
Nifty is about to close for a trading holiday
body.explanation: A sharp IV jump with no accompanying move in the underlying is the classic signature of event risk being priced in ahead of time. Realized volatility cannot see the future event coming since it only measures what already happened; implied volatility exists specifically to price exactly this kind of known, dated uncertainty.

body.title: Karthik's Budget-day options trade
body.scenario: Karthik buys a Nifty weekly ATM straddle two days before the Union Budget, paying a combined premium of ₹640, expecting a big move either way. On Budget day, Nifty actually swings a sharp 380 points intraday before closing 210 points higher than the previous close. Karthik is right that a big move happened, but when he checks his straddle that evening, it is worth only ₹510, a loss of ₹130.
body.prompt: Using what you know about IV crush and expected move, explain why Karthik lost money on a straddle even though a genuinely large move occurred.
body.modelAnswer: The straddle's ₹640 entry price already had a large move baked in. With ATM IV elevated to price Budget-day event risk, the expected move implied by that premium was likely close to or above the 380-point intraday swing Karthik actually got. The moment the Budget was announced and the event risk resolved, IV collapsed back toward its normal level, the IV crush, and that collapse in the volatility input pulled the straddle's value down faster than the delta gains from the 210-point closing move could offset. Karthik was right that volatility would happen, but he paid a price that already assumed it would, so the move needed to be bigger than what IV had already priced in for him to profit.

body.title: Historical Volatility vs Implied Volatility, Side by Side

columns.label: Historical (Realized) Volatility
points: Computed from actual past price returns
Purely backward-looking, a statistic on data that already exists
Same number for everyone; no option prices involved
Cannot see a scheduled event coming
Changes only as slowly as new daily data arrives

columns.label: Implied Volatility
points: Backed out from a live option's market price
Forward-looking, reflects expectations for the remaining life of the option
Different for every strike and expiry (the subject of Chapters 2 and 3)
Prices in known events, such as the Budget, results, or RBI policy, well in advance
Can jump or collapse within minutes as the option price moves

body.text: Historical volatility tells you how rough the road has been. Implied volatility tells you how much the market is charging you, right now, to travel the road ahead. They describe the same underlying, but they answer two different questions, and every serious options decision depends on knowing which one you are actually looking at.

points: Historical (realized) volatility is the annualized standard deviation of past daily returns: purely backward-looking arithmetic with no option prices involved.
Implied volatility is backed out from a live option premium by inverting the pricing model; it is forward-looking and exists only because a market price already exists.
India VIX is NSE's aggregate implied volatility measure, built from the bid-ask quotes of near and next-month Nifty options, representing expected 30-day volatility, not a measure of past moves.
On average, IV trades a little above subsequently realized volatility: the volatility risk premium (VRP); it compresses or reverses around known events.
Known events like the Union Budget push IV sharply higher in advance, then IV crush can hit right after the event resolves, even when the underlying makes a large move.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All Nifty levels, IV figures, and the Karthik scenario are hypothetical and illustrative, built to explain the mechanics of historical versus implied volatility, not to represent live NSE data. Always pull real numbers from NSE, India VIX's official page, or your broker's terminal (such as Zerodha Kite or Sensibull) before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
